title.narrative: UNFPA: Addressing the needs of women and girls in the regional Syria crisis
UNFPA: Att ta itu med kvinnors och flickors behov i den regionala Syrien-krisen

description.narrative:
Den föreslagna programplaneringen omfattar perioden från 1 januari 2021 till 31 december 2023 och är en fortsättning på samma program som tidigare har finansierats för Syrien, Jordanien, Libanon, Turkiet och Turkiet gränsöverskridande av the United Nations Population Fund(UNFPA). Den totala budgeten för programmet omfattar 180 000 000 SEK (20031,15 MUSD) och har fyra huvudmålsättningar:
- Öka tillgängligheten och tillgången till specialiserade och integrerade SRH- och GBV-tjänster, särskilt för kvinnor, flickor och personer med funktionsnedsättning.
- Förbättra kapaciteten för de tjänster som levereras och hos samarbetsspartners för att tillhandahålla högkvalitativa, inkluderande och omfattande GBV- och RH-tjänster.
- Utmana de negativa sociala normerna som förhindrar stärkandet av kvinnors och flickors rättigheter.
- Öka dialogen med regeringar, grupper, samhällen och andra intressenter för att förbättra skyddet för och hälsan hos kvinnor, flickor, ungdomar och andra utsatta grupper.

In the proposed programming from 01 January 2021 till 31 December 2023 is a continuation of the same programe that has been funded previously covering Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Turkey and Turkey cross border implemented by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). The budget is 180 000 000 SEK 820,031,15 MUSD) and has four main objectives:
- Increase the availability of and access to specialized and integrated SRH and GBV services, especially for women, girls, and persons with disabilities.
- Improve capacity of service and implementing partners to provide high-quality, inclusive, and comprehensive GBV and RH services.
- Challenge the negative social norms that prevent the empowerment of women and girls.
- Increase advocacy efforts with governments, advocacy groups, communities, and other stakeholders to improve the protection and health of women, girls, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

The proposed UNFPA Programme:Addressing the needs of women and girls in the regional Syria crisis seeks to achieve an overall goal to increase the sense of well being of women and girls accessing UNFPA programmes and supported services (including WGSS, Youth programmes, Health facilities) and activities. The specific objectives are: 1) Increase the availability of and access to specialised and integrated SRH and GBV services, especially for women, girls, and persons with disabilities. 2) Improve capacity of service and implementing partners to provide high-quality, inclusive, and comprehensive GBV and RH services. 3) Challenge the negative social norms that prevent the empowerment of women and girls. 4) Increase advocacy efforts with governments, advocacy groups, communities, and other stakeholders to improve the protection and health of women, girls, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

description.narrative:
Overall results (2021-2025)
Objective one: Increase the availability of and access to specialised and integrated SRH and GBV services, especially for women, girls, and persons with disabilities
- Reached 559,363 persons with SRH services and 383,900 with GBV services (of which, 275,149 people with SRH services and 165,692 with GBV services in Syria).
- UNFPA Syria provided comprehensive and specialized GBV services through seven static Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSSs) located in Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor (DEZ), Homs, Rural Damascus, and Damascus. These WGSSs offered a range of integrated and comprehensive services, including Awareness-raising sessions on GBV prevention and response GBV case management for survivors, Individual and group psychosocial support (PSS) for women and girls, including GBV survivors, and Vocational training, resilience building, and income-generation skills enhancement, which contributed to reducing GBV risks associated with economic vulnerability
Objective two: Improve capacity of service and implementing partners to provide high-quality, inclusive, and comprehensive GBV and RH services.
- Between 2021 and 2025, UNFPA Syria trained a total of 5,377 service providers on SRH and 3,528 on GBV, thereby strengthening the overall quality of service provision. The capacity-building programme significantly contributed to improving the quality of services, as reflected by a 95% user satisfaction rate with the services provided.
Objective three: Challenge the negative social norms that prevent the empowerment of women and girls.
- The expansion of the Adolescent Mothers Against All Odds (AMAL) initiative through the Turkyie cross-border operation, reaching 1,833 adolescent girls and establishing Young Mothers Clubs for 2,209 beneficiaries, signifies a growing and targeted approach to specific vulnerable groups.
Objective four: Increase advocacy efforts with governments, advocacy groups, communities, and other stakeholders to improve the protection and health of women, girls, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.
- UNFPA, in partnership with the Syrian Commission for Family Affairs and Population (SCFAP), advanced gender equality in Syria by promoting legal reforms and strengthening institutional capacity. An advocacy workshop for 103 judges and trainee judges highlighted the judiciarys role in eliminating discriminatory laws, while an updated study analyzed key legal instruments and gaps affecting women, offering concrete recommendations for reform. Simultaneously, UNFPA trained 667 government stakeholders on gender-sensitive data collection, enhancing the use of sex-disaggregated and gender-sensitive indicators to inform evidence-based policies and decision-making. Together, these initiatives strengthened legal, institutional, and data frameworks to support more equitable and effective programming for women and girls.
Context
Between 2021 and 2025, the humanitarian situation in the Syrian Arab Republic and the wider Syria crisis region was marked by a confluence of protracted conflict, economic collapse, pandemic-related shocks, climate stressors, natural disasters, and major political transition. By the end of 2024, an estimated 16.7 million people in Syria were in need of humanitarian assistancethe highest figure since the conflict began in 2011. Among these, more than 8 million were women and girls, approximately 4 million of reproductive age (Humanitarian Needs Overview Syria HNO, 2025).
Throughout the duration of the project, the political and security landscape were influenced firstly by the February 2023 earthquake and then by the major political shift in December 2024, when the Assad regime fell. Against the background of this fragile environment, UNFPA, supported by Sweden as well as other partners, contributed to ensuring safe and protected access to integrated sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response services, operationalizing womens and girls safe spaces (WGSS), deploying integrated mobile teams (IMTs), and providing life-saving cash and voucher assistance. Despite the complexities of operating in a rapidly evolving scenario, with operational challenges across all of the countries targeted by this initiative, UNFPA contributed to strengthening health systems, supported legal reforms advancing gender equality, and sustained services for displaced and conflict-affected populations.
Amidst this highly volatile context and throughout the duration of the project, the situation in Northwest Syria (NWS) remained particularly dire, marked by prolonged conflict, mass displacement, and systemic GBV risks in overcrowded camps where 80% of residents are women and children. Over 4.1 million people required humanitarian assistance in 2024, with 2.1 million in need of GBV services (Syria Humanitarian Needs Overview, 2024). Women and girls, especially widows, adolescents, and displaced persons, faced increased exposure to intimate partner violence, child marriage, and resource deprivation. The proposed morality law in Idlib threatened to further restrict their rights and access to services, while ongoing hostilities damaged health facilities, including UNFPA-supported maternity care. In the immediate aftermath of escalations, UNFPA reached nearly 185,000 people with SRH and GBV services, but insecurity, shortages of staff and supplies, and destruction of health infrastructure continued to hinder service delivery.
Regional spillovers magnified the crisis. In Jordan, which hosts the second-highest number of Syrian refugees per capita globally, the protracted Syrian conflict strained national resources and services. By mid-2025, over half a million Syrian refugees were registered in Jordan, the majority in host communities. With Swedens crucial support, UNFPA enabled more than 90,000 people to access SRH services and over 63,000 to benefit from GBV services, while strengthening youth engagement and supporting nine WGSSs and nine SRH facilities.
Throughout the reporting period, Lebanon remained engulfed in a compounded socioeconomic and political crisis. More than 80% of its population lived in poverty, with 1.5 million Syrian refugees among the most vulnerable. By late 2024, escalating violence displaced 1.2 million people, leaving hundreds of thousands in overcrowded shelters with limited access to health, protection, and social services. GBV risks surged, with women and girls making up 98% of reported survivors, primarily facing physical assault, psychological abuse, and forced marriage. Simultaneously, the health system faced collapse, with hospitals and facilities destroyed, healthcare workers killed or displaced, and maternal and reproductive health services severely disrupted. The embassy prolonged its support to the end of March 2025 to provide much-needed assistance to IDPs.
In Türkiye, which remained the worlds largest refugee-hosting country, UNFPA adapted to growing needs amid rising social tensions, economic instability, and restrictive policies. Following the 2023 earthquakes that displaced over 1.7 million people, UNFPA rapidly scaled up emergency SRH and GBV interventions, deploying mobile clinics and expanding outreach, including through SIDA-funded WGSSs in the affected provinces. By 2024, programming began transitioning to early recovery, with gradual handovers to local actors. However, sharp funding cuts forced downsizing and reduced coverage, even as humanitarian needs remained acute.
Across all contexts, women and girls bore the brunt of conflict, displacement, and socioeconomic collapse. GBV risks escalated while access to SRH services, protection mechanisms, and livelihood opportunities declined. Despite immense operational challenges, UNFPA and its partners remained on the frontlines delivering life-saving services, strengthening systems, and advancing gender equality in some of the worlds most protracted and complex crises.
Overall achievements and programmatic lessons learned from the partner
A notable development was the significant increase in health workers trained on GBV basics, indicating a systematic effort to embed GBV awareness across health services. While direct social norms interventions faced initial challenges, the AMAL initiative's success in shifting unequal gender and power norms highlights an adaptive learning process and a growing capacity to implement transformative approaches in sensitive environments.
Across the programme areas, 95% of sampled individuals expressed satisfaction with the quality of support provided, highlighting the relevance and appropriateness of the interventions. Furthermore, 97% reported that the services received had a positive impact on their lives, underscoring the programmes effectiveness in addressing urgent protection and health needs. The programme also emphasized community engagement and accountability to affected populations. Around 91% of individuals surveyed reported having positive opportunities to provide feedback on the services they received.
Operating a multi-country program addressing gender-based violence (GBV) and sexual and reproductive health (SRH) across Syria, Lebanon, Turkey, Jordan, and northwest Syria has yielded crucial regional insights. Some of these include,
- Adaptability and Flexible Service Delivery: Mobile integrated teams and community outreach were vital for maintaining access to services amidst volatile political, economic, and security conditions. This approach ensured continued support during crises like the 2023 earthquake, the 2024 Lebanon displacement, and shifting government structures in Syria.
- Strong Local Partnerships: National NGOs, women-led organizations, and community leaders were foundational in contextualizing interventions, building trust, and reaching underserved populations.
- Inclusive Programming: Tailored strategies, including peer outreach, sign language interpretation, and services adapted for persons with disabilities, significantly improved accessibility and equity.
- Multi-Stakeholder Coordination: Both national and regional coordination mechanisms enhanced program coherence and policy impact, especially when government counterparts were actively engaged.
- Staff Well-being and Capacity Building: Investment in staff well-being, technical supervision, and capacity building was critical for mitigating burnout and high turnover in protracted crises.
- Donor Flexibility and Rapid Reprogramming: Donor flexibility and the capacity for rapid reprogramming enabled timely, needs-based responses.
- Integrated Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA): Support such as transport stipends and cash for dignity kits significantly increased safe access to services.
- Feedback Mechanisms and Evidence-Informed Adaptations: Consistent use of feedback mechanisms and evidence-informed adjustments, from revising group sessions to optimizing outreach timing, ensured services remained responsive, relevant, and trusted by communities amidst continuous disruption.
